newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish government hopes to get its way with taxes.
newsitem.headline: Polish government hopes to get its way with taxes.

text.p: The Polish government hopes to defend its moderate tax cut proposals for next year in the Senate and overturn last week's lower house decision to slash taxes for the low paid, Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko said.
"We want to persuade the Senate to overturn what has been unfortunately passed in the Sejm (lower house)," Kolodko told a news conference on Monday.

On Thursday the co-ruling Polish Peasant Party (PSL) unexpectedly joined forces with the opposition against its coalition partner, the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), to introduce a new lower tax band at 17 percent.
The government had announced plans to cut taxes next year, but only to 20, 31 and 43 percent levels.

But in a shock defeat for the government, the chamber approved a bill setting next year's tax levels at 17, 20, 33 and 45 percent from the current 21, 33 and 45 percent, despite finance ministry warnings that the move would cost the budget about 4.6 billion zlotys ($1.63 billion) in lost revenues.

The Peasants later suggested they might agree to block the bill in the Senate if their experts are convinced the plan to slash taxes for the lowest paid could not be accommodated by the nearly-complete 1997 budget.

Kolodko said the government, bound by an October 31 deadline, would submit to parliament on Tuesday a budget draft based on this year's tax levels and assuming a deficit of 11.3 billion zlotys or 2.6 percent of gross domestic product.
But he said the government would prepare amendments to the budget bill if the parliament approves its tax cut proposals.
"The budget draft approved today assumes a 2.6 percent deficit, which given its structure of revenues and spending is possible to finance," Kolodko said.
"If the Senate approves the government (tax) proposal the government will submit necessary amendments to parliament," he added.
Last week, when presenting the government's proposals for tax cuts, Kolodko said the lower taxes would require the deficit to widen to 2.8 percent of GDP - the deficit target for this year.

The Senate is scheduled to hold a one-day session on Wednesday, October 30, but the tax debate is not on its agenda and the vote on tax bills is expected to be held during next week's session, likely to start on November 6.
